newsitem.title: MEXICO: FORECAST - Mexican December CPI seen up 3.47 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Mexican December CPI seen up 3.47 pct.

text.p: Mexican inflation in December is expected to be 3.47 percent, fueled by sharp rises in tortilla and milk prices, economists said on Wednesday.

The average forecast of six Mexico City-based economists was 3.47 percent, with forecasts ranging from 3.4 percent to 3.65 percent. Consumer Price Index data are due to be released around 1430 local (2030 GMT) on Thursday.
Most analysts expect annual inflation to be around 28 percent, well above the government's 1996 target of 20.5 percent.

They were forced to push up their estimates in December after inflation in the first half of the month was a higher- than-expected 2.34 percent -- a level almost as high as some economists had forecast for the whole month. That rise was spurred by sharp rises in transport costs in Mexico City, as well as gasoline increases nationwide, Banco de Mexico said.

In the second half of the month, the government raised the controlled prices of tortilla and milk by around 20 percent and 11 percent, respectively, which economists said would put steep upward pressure on the price of the basic basket of goods that is a major component of the CPI.

Analysts said the only shock in the report would be if those price rises push the index sharply above a 3.5 percent rise. Otherwise it is likely to be shrugged off by the markets, which are convinced the blip is nothing more than seasonal.

"It is more important to look at interest rates," said Hector Velez, economist at Inverlat, who has the highest inflation projection at 3.65 percent. He expected inflation to hit 3.5 percent in January, also higher than the market consensus, though he says the trend is downward.
His concern was that interest rates on Cetes were falling so fast they may provide negative real returns.
For example, assuming an average Cetes rate of 26 percent in January and a 3.5 percent inflation rate, the negative real return would be above 10 percent, Velez said.
